strengths: Interesting and timely central idea: repurposing generative decoders, including Stable Diffusion and MAE decoders, for category-agnostic instance segmentation via a simple image-to-image formulation.
The instance coloring objective is simple and well motivated, and the paper shows it can be applied across multiple generative backbones rather than only one diffusion model.

Evaluation spans several out-of-distribution settings, including COCO excluded categories, art, egocentric images, fine structures, and X-ray imagery; the comparison to SAM, SimpleClick trained on the same synthetic data, and a DINO-based variant is informative.

The strongest SD model achieves surprisingly competitive single-point prompt IoU on large COCO objects and DRAM, and clearly outperforms SAM on iShape, supporting the claim that generative features can capture fine structures and boundaries.
The appendix includes useful implementation details, an ablation of the loss components, category lists, and randomly sampled qualitative pages, which improves reproducibility and interpretability.
weaknesses: The main claim that generative pretraining inherently learns transferable instance grouping is not fully isolated. The models are fine-tuned on 86k synthetic images and 3.7M masks, and the comparisons do not include random initialization or stronger non-generative/self-supervised segmentation baselines that would better separate pretraining, architecture, decoder, and supervision effects.

The evaluation is mostly prompt-based with oracle object-center points, so it does not demonstrate full automatic instance segmentation quality using standard AP, AR, PQ, proposal recall, or whole-image mask generation metrics.

Claims of approaching SAM are somewhat overstated: performance is very weak on small COCO objects, substantially below SAM on several datasets, and the multi-prompt curve excludes COCO medium/small objects, which hides an important failure mode.

Baseline coverage is limited. SimpleClick trained only on the narrow synthetic data and a relatively ad hoc DINO+VAE model may be weak representatives of discriminative/self-supervised approaches; stronger category-agnostic, open-world, or unsupervised segmentation methods are missing.

The novelty of the loss is not well positioned relative to prior discriminative embedding/instance-separation losses, associative embeddings, and instance-coloring formulations, making the methodological contribution feel more incremental than the framing suggests.

The “unseen categories” framing is complicated by broad visual pretraining and by Hypersim unknown-category masks; SD-Limited helps but does not fully resolve possible category or domain leakage, especially for MAE/ImageNet and Stable Diffusion pretraining.

Quantitative reporting is fairly thin: no confidence intervals, limited dataset-size details in the main text, limited per-category/per-size analysis beyond COCO L/M/S, and no runtime or memory comparison at inference.

strengths: Interesting and timely premise: adapting generative image models, including Stable Diffusion and MAE encoder-decoder models, to category-agnostic instance segmentation via an instance-coloring objective is a clear and potentially impactful contribution.

The paper evaluates across several out-of-distribution datasets and domains, including COCO excluded categories, art, egocentric images, irregular structures, X-rays, and BSDS500 edges, which gives more evidence than a narrow single-dataset study.

The empirical results are promising: SD and MAE variants substantially outperform the trained SimpleClick and DINO baselines, approach SAM on several single-point prompt settings, and clearly exceed SAM on iShape/fine-structure examples.
The method is conceptually simple and well motivated, with useful implementation details and an ablation showing that the variance and separation losses matter.
The MAE results are especially valuable because they weaken the explanation that performance comes only from Stable Diffusion's internet-scale pretraining or text conditioning.
weaknesses: The main claims are stronger than the evidence. The paper argues that generative models inherently learn general object grouping, but the experiments do not fully disentangle generative pretraining from architecture, decoder capacity, resolution, data scale, or target-domain exposure during pretraining.

The evaluation is not a complete instance segmentation evaluation. Most quantitative evidence uses ground-truth center-point prompting and mIoU, rather than mask AP, PQ, ARI, object discovery, proposal quality, or automatic instance segmentation metrics.

Baselines are useful but incomplete. DINO-B plus a simple VAE connector is a weak representative of discriminative/self-supervised features, and SimpleClick is trained at low resolution; stronger feature-clustering, open-vocabulary, diffusion-feature, SAM/SAM2 variants, and resolution-matched discriminative baselines are missing.

The zero-shot/category-exclusion story is somewhat fragile: Hypersim has a very large 'unknown' category, Stable Diffusion may have seen many target domains during pretraining, and manual verification of absent categories is not enough to support broad 'never seen' language.

The SAM comparison should be interpreted cautiously. The paper selectively excludes COCO medium/small objects in some plots, uses different training resolutions, and emphasizes cases where SAM underperforms while SAM remains much stronger on small objects and several datasets.
Ablations are limited to one dataset/model setting and do not report variance across seeds, threshold sensitivity, prompt sensitivity, resolution effects, or dataset-composition effects.

Reproducibility is only partly supported in the manuscript: it mentions code/models/demos but does not provide a concrete URL in the text, and some optimizer/evaluation details and dataset filtering scripts are not fully specified.

The paper lacks a meaningful limitations/ethics discussion despite discussing applications in robotics, medical imaging, security X-rays, and autonomous systems, where segmentation failures and dataset biases can matter.

strengths: The paper poses an interesting and timely question: whether generative image models contain transferable grouping structure that can be repurposed for instance segmentation with limited mask supervision.

The evaluation covers several out-of-distribution domains, including art, egocentric images, irregular shapes, and X-ray imagery, which is a useful stress test for category generalization.

The comparisons to same-data SimpleClick and DINO-based baselines provide evidence that the gains are not merely due to synthetic supervised training, and the ablation study supports the main loss components.
Qualitative results are compelling in some cases, especially for fine structures where SAM appears to over- or under-segment.
weaknesses: The central claims are stronger than the evidence. The method approaches SAM only in selected settings; it substantially underperforms on COCO medium/small objects, EgoHOS, and PIDRay, and several headline statements exclude the hardest cases.

The evaluation protocol is narrow for an instance segmentation paper: it relies heavily on promptable segmentation with ground-truth center clicks and does not report standard mask proposal or instance segmentation metrics such as AP, PQ, ARI, object discovery quality, or automatic instance extraction performance.

The novelty is moderate. The loss resembles classic discriminative embedding pull-push objectives for instance segmentation, and the RGB colorization framing is an implementation choice rather than a clearly new technical mechanism.

The baseline set is incomplete for the claims. Relevant unsupervised, class-agnostic, object discovery, open-world, and promptable segmentation methods are missing, and the DINO+VAE baseline is somewhat artificial.

The zero-shot framing is not fully convincing. Stable Diffusion has internet-scale pretraining that may include many target categories and possibly similar evaluation images, while the claim that MAE has not seen domains such as art or X-rays is asserted rather than empirically established.

There are important confounds in resolution, architecture, and supervision. SAM is evaluated off-the-shelf at high resolution, MAE/DINO/SimpleClick at 224 resolution, and SD at different resolutions, making attribution to generative pretraining difficult.
The prompt-to-mask decoding uses fixed heuristic thresholds and smoothing, but sensitivity to these choices, dataset-specific tuning, and robustness are not sufficiently analyzed.

The paper would benefit from clearer reproducibility details for the evaluation pipeline, variance across seeds, per-dataset sample counts after filtering, and failure-mode analysis beyond qualitative examples.

The method is simple, architecture-agnostic, and relatively efficient compared with training SAM-scale systems, which makes the contribution easy to understand and likely reproducible if the promised code and checkpoints are released.
weaknesses: The main claims are somewhat stronger than the evidence. The results show that generative backbones are useful after supervised mask finetuning, but they do not fully establish that generative pretraining inherently learns a general object-grouping mechanism; alternative explanations such as decoder resolution, synthetic boundary quality, or pretraining category exposure are not completely ruled out.

The comparison to SAM is uneven. The proposed method is close to or better than SAM in selected regimes, but it is far behind on medium and especially small COCO objects and notably below SAM on EgoHOS and PIDRay. Statements that the model closely approaches SAM should be qualified more carefully.

The evaluation is centered on point-prompt IoU and a nonstandard edge metric restricted to AP below 20% recall. This is useful diagnostically, but standard instance segmentation metrics, automatic mask generation metrics, full PR/average precision, and multi-point interactive curves should be more prominent.

The training data is described as narrow, but Hypersim contains a very large 'unknown' category with instance masks, and Stable Diffusion/MAE pretraining likely contains many evaluation object types as images. The paper should more carefully separate 'unseen masks/categories during finetuning' from 'unseen visual concepts'.

The baselines are helpful but incomplete. Stronger or more directly comparable baselines using diffusion/MAE features, SAM2/HQ-SAM variants, open-vocabulary/generalist segmenters, and simple frozen-feature clustering or embedding-loss baselines would clarify how much of the gain comes from generative pretraining versus the particular output/loss/prompting pipeline.

The method has clear limitations on small objects and crowded scenes, and the RGB embedding formulation plus fixed thresholding may be brittle or resolution-sensitive; these limitations are acknowledged but not deeply analyzed.
